findings.title: Minimum token schema strips required token fields
findings.body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not create catch-all Zod fields. The resulting object schema therefore only retains `access_token` and strips fields such as `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type`, and the real `refresh_token` when credential sharing is enabled. Callers that persist or consume the parsed data lose expiry and refresh information and can store unusable credentials.

findings.title: Missing refresh token is replaced with a literal placeholder
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, this code sets it to the literal string `"refresh_token"`. Zoom's adapter copies `newTokens.refresh_token` into the stored credential and Google/Office flows can persist the parsed result, so the real refresh token is overwritten by a placeholder. The next refresh will fail and the user must reconnect the app.

findings.title: Google credential update stores the SafeParse wrapper instead of token data
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the Zod `SafeParseReturnType` object (`{success, data}`), but this code assigns that whole object to `key` and writes it to `prisma.credential.update`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse` returned the credential object itself. The stored key becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}`, so the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` will fail because the token fields are nested under `data`.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file has no `prisma` import (imports only include `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). Every Salesforce client construction will throw a ReferenceError after the token request, breaking the integration entirely.

findings.title: Salesforce client is built with the old access token
findings.body: After fetching and parsing a refreshed token, `getClient` constructs the jsforce Connection with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` and `refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token` from the pre-refresh credential instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. If the old token was expired, the returned client still carries the expired token and Salesforce calls will fail despite the refresh.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response incompatible with most callers
findings.body: When sync is enabled this returns the raw `fetch` Response without checking `response.ok` or parsing JSON, while the fallback returns whatever the app-specific refresh function returns (HubSpot token object, axios response, Google token response, etc.). Callers such as HubSpot (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn/accessToken`), Zoho CRM/Bigin (`tokenInfo.data.*`), and Office365Video expect those app-specific shapes, so with sync enabled they read undefined fields, compute NaN expiries, and persist broken credentials instead of using the synced access token.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens`' third parameter is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. This call passes `credentialId` (the credential primary key) instead. The parent platform will look up the wrong user (or no user) and return another user's/no tokens, so synced Zoho Bigin refreshes cannot work correctly and could cross users.

findings.title: Office365 refresh loses expiry transformation under sync schema
findings.body: With sync enabled `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses the minimum schema, which strips `expires_in` instead of applying `refreshTokenResponseSchema`'s transform of `expires_in` into an absolute expiry timestamp. The merged credential written at line 265 keeps the old expired `expires_in`, and `getToken` at line 278 checks `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(...).success && !isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`, so the credential is treated as permanently expired and refreshed on every call.

findings.title: Zoom expiry becomes NaN with sync token parsing
findings.body: Under sync parsing `expires_in` is stripped from `newTokens`, so `Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` evaluates to NaN and is stored as `key.expiry_date` at line 124, together with the placeholder refresh token from `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. The persisted Zoom credential is corrupted and `zoomTokenSchema.parse` on the next `getToken` call will reject it.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with non-constant-time equality
findings.body: The shared secret that authorizes writing arbitrary third-party credentials for any userId is checked with `!==` on the header value. This is vulnerable to timing side-channel disclosure of the secret; the comparison should use a length-checked `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. A leaked secret allows an attacker to overwrite any user's app credentials.

findings.title: Webhook handler has no error handling for invalid body or decrypt failures
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` at line 31 and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` at lines 57-59 throw on malformed JSON, a wrong encryption key, or non-JSON plaintext. There is no try/catch and no HTTP method check, so bad requests produce unhandled 500s (and stack/error leakage depending on runtime config) instead of a controlled 400 response, making integration failures hard to distinguish from server faults.
